EP01.ig:
How does a $200K offer turn into a $1M deal?

He asked for $100K for 10%, a $1M valuation. Kevin opened at 50%, valuing the company at $200K. Then Daymond and Lori jumped in, and the price climbed. Final deal: $200K for 20%. Exactly his ask, and five times the first offer.

The sponge didn't change. The numbers didn't change. Competition did.

One buyer sets the price. Several buyers fight over it. That's why good M&A advisors run a process: multiple buyers, one deadline.

EP02.ig:
Kevin offered $100K and let him keep 100% of the company. It may have been the most expensive offer in the room.

It's a royalty: 50¢ a sponge until the $100K is paid back, then 10¢ a sponge forever. On a sponge that costs about $1 to make, that comes off the top, before payroll and rent. At 50M sponges a year, that's $5M a year for one check.

And a royalty that never ends doesn't disappear when you sell. Buyers treat it like debt. They cut your price or make you buy it out first.

Compare offers by what they cost you over time, not the size of the check.

EP04.ig:
Kevin wanted 50 cents for every cupcake they'd ever sell. Forever. They said yes... almost.

Wicked Good Cupcakes asked for $75K for 20%. Kevin offered $75K with zero equity: $1 a jar until repaid, then 50 cents forever. They settled at 45 cents and kept 100% of the company.

It paid off. Then Hickory Farms bought the business, and the royalty came with it.

A royalty isn't good or bad. It's a cost. Price it before you sign it.

EP05.ig:
They gave up 3.5x the equity they came in to sell, and it may be the best deal ever made in the Tank.

Bombas asked for $200K for 5%. Daymond pushed to 20%. The founders countered: 15% plus a $200K line of credit. They closed at 17.5% plus inventory financing.

A sock company doesn't die from a low valuation. It dies from running out of cash between buying inventory and getting paid.

Don't just negotiate the price. Negotiate what the money does.

EP07.ig:
All five Sharks bought in. One million dollars. Four years later, the FTC said the product didn't do what it promised.

Breathometer asked for $250K for 10%. A bidding war pushed it to $1M for 30% from all five Sharks. The price went up because everyone wanted in. Nobody stopped to ask: does it actually work?

In 2017 the FTC said the company knew its devices often under-reported blood alcohol while advertising them as accurate. The company settled without admitting the allegations.

In real M&A, a buyer doesn't just buy revenue. They buy every promise the company ever made. Hype raises the price, not the safety.

EP08.ig:
Mark Cuban offered $30 million for the whole company. They said no without blinking.

Coffee Meets Bagel asked for $500K for 5%, a $10M valuation. Mark came back with $30M for 100%: three times their own price, all cash, no dilution.

They said no, and raised nearly $20M from investors afterward. But every round meant selling more of the company.

Was it the right call? An offer isn't just a price. Weigh it against the risk, the dilution, and the years it takes to beat it.

EP09.ig:
A grocery giant paid a reported $200M for a meal kit company. Two years later, it shut the service down.

Plated asked for $500K for 4%. Mark shook on 5.5% plus advisory shares, then the deal fell apart after the show. In 2017, Amazon bought Whole Foods and Albertsons bought Plated in the panic. By 2019 it had written down $38M, most of it the brand itself.

For sellers: timing is value. For buyers: fear is not a valuation.

EP10.ig:
Two Sharks wanted control of this bagel company for $275K. It later sold for $34M.

Bantam Bagels asked for $275K for 11%. Barbara wanted 51%. Kevin wanted 50%. That's not an investment. That's control.

They made a deal with Lori instead, landed QVC, grocery freezers and Starbucks, and in 2018 sold to T. Marzetti for $34M on about $20M in annual sales. In 2022 the new owner discontinued the brand. Once you sell, the buyer decides what lives.

Early money is the most expensive money. Never sell control just to get started.
